comments.author: Matthew Coombs
comments.comment: The autonomy ladder I use is: can this fail safely without a human watching every step? If the answer is no, I usually keep it as retrieval, extraction, or copilot flow first, then add agent behavior only around the smallest repeatable subtask.

comments.author: Alok Sharan
comments.comment: The trap I see is treating “agent memory” as one box, when production systems usually need at least three: short-term state, long-term user/context memory, and audit/history for debugging. Those have different latency, privacy, retention, and retrieval requirements. A good architecture decision is often deciding what not to remember.

comments.author: Naresh Edagotti
comments.comment: The hardest production agent bug is often not the model, it is missing state boundaries. I’d expect a strong answer to start with trace IDs, tool-call budgets, idempotency, retry policy, and eval sets built from real failure cases, because “same prompt, different result” is rarely debugged from the prompt alone.

comments.author: Luca Torresi
comments.comment: The hard part is not spinning up a cloud desktop agent, it is constraining what it can do once it has GUI access. I’d be curious how you handle permissioning, audit logs, and recovery when the agent clicks the wrong thing in a real user session.

comments.author: Kobi Omenaka
comments.comment: The first unlock for me was treating Claude Code like a junior dev with repo access, not like a chatbot. Start with tiny scoped tasks, ask it to explain the diff before applying, and keep git status visible the whole time.
